cases.question: Our Group R-2 building has a scissor stair with the two stair entrance doors located 15 feet apart. Can the two stairs be counted as two separate exits?
cases.reviewNote: The conditional two-exit answer preserves the general rule, both two-hour construction requirements, masonry/equivalent condition and 15-foot minimum. It accepts the stated occupancy and separation and identifies only unresolved construction facts. Yes conditionally is substantively consistent with the reference; exact opening words are not the scoring criterion.

reviewedAnswer.answerText:
**Yes—conditionally.** In a Group R-2 occupancy, the two stairs in a scissor-stair assembly may be counted as two exit stairways even though they share the scissor enclosure, if (1) each stair is enclosed by walls with at least a 2-hour fire-resistance rating and constructed of masonry or masonry equivalent in accordance with department rules, (2) the construction separating the two stairs also has at least a 2-hour fire-resistance rating and is masonry or masonry equivalent in accordance with department rules, and (3) the two exit doors are at least 15 feet apart. Your stated 15-foot door separation satisfies the stated minimum. (BC § 1007.1.1, Exception 3.)

Absent that Group R-2 exception, stairs sharing a common wall, floor, ceiling, scissor-stair assembly, or other enclosure count as one exit stairway. The supplied evidence does not establish whether the required 2-hour masonry-or-masonry-equivalent enclosures and separating construction are provided, so the final count remains conditional on those construction conditions.

cases.question: A new natural-gas piping system in a Manhattan commercial building will operate at 15 psig. Can it be designed only under the ordinary Fuel Gas Code piping provisions, without considering Appendix G?
cases.reviewNote: The Appendix G conclusion at exactly 15 psig is correct. The answer adds interior-pressure, testing and appliance-flow checks that are unnecessary to that threshold decision, and contains the malformed word installation[]. Retained conversation facts incorrectly turn a new piping system in a commercial building into a new-construction building; the same error reproduces in the current local fact extractor.

reviewedAnswer.answerText:
**No.** At **15 psig**, the system is a high pressure natural gas installation[] at pressures of 15 psig … or above, so it must also comply with **Appendix G**; the ordinary Fuel Gas Code piping provisions alone are not sufficient (FGC § 101.2.2).

If the 15-psig piping is located inside the building, the ordinary maximum is 1/2 psig. The stated 15-psig level is permitted only for appliances exceeding 100,000 cubic feet per hour, provided the distribution piping is installed under FGC § 404 (FGC § 402.6, Exception 2). That conditional permission does not remove the separate Appendix G requirement. Before service, the piping must be gas-tight tested, and prior to acceptance and initial operation it must be inspected and pressure-tested for compliance with the code’s materials, design, fabrication, and installation requirements (FGC §§ 404.20, 406.1). The supplied evidence does not include Appendix G’s text, so its specific design requirements cannot be identified here.

cases.question: A gas system has a proposed maximum working pressure of 2 psig. The contractor proposes to test it at 2 psig because that equals the operating pressure. Is that test pressure sufficient?
cases.reviewNote: The ordinary 1.5 times 2 = 3 psig result and the separate higher/special testing conditions are supported. The answer keeps ordinary test duration unresolved. The general measurement procedure, repeated special-case checklist and supporting-point duplication can be shortened without deleting material exceptions.

reviewedAnswer.answerText:
**No.** A 2-psig test is insufficient for a gas system with a proposed maximum working pressure of 2 psig. The required test pressure is at least 1½ times the proposed maximum working pressure, but never less than 3 psig: 1.5 × 2 psig = **3 psig**, which is the required minimum here (FGC § 406.4.1). The test must use air or an inert gas, with the pressure source isolated before readings are taken; the system must be tested and proven tight before appliances are connected (FGC §§ 406.4.1, 406.4).

This conclusion assumes none of the stated higher/special test categories applies. In particular, piping in a public corridor under § 404 requires 10 psig for at least 30 minutes; coated and wrapped pipe requires at least 100 psig for at least 60 minutes; and meter piping follows the serving utility’s requirements (FGC § 406.4.1).

The required test pressure is at least 1½ times the proposed maximum working pressure, but never less than 3 psig: 1.5 × 2 psig = **3 psig**, which is the required minimum here (FGC § 406.4.1). The test must use air or an inert gas, with the pressure source isolated before readings are taken; the system must be tested and proven tight before appliances are connected (FGC §§ 406.4.1, 406.4).

supportedPoints.explanation: Before appliances are connected, the completed gas-system section or system must be verified as to materials and tested and proven tight. supportingPassages.selectedText: 406.4.1 406.4.1 Test pressure. The test pressure to be used shall be not less than 1 1/2 times the proposed maximum working pressure, but not less than 3 psig (20.9 kPa gauge), irrespective of design pressure. Where the test pressure exceeds 125 psig (861.8 kPa gauge), the test pressure shall not exceed a value that produces a hoop stress in the piping greater than 50 percent of the specified minimum yield strength of the pipe. Notwithstanding the above, all field applied or factory applied coated and wrapped pipe shall be pressure tested at a minimum of 100 psig (689.5 kPa gauge) for a minimum of 60 minutes. All test duration time periods are to be measured after stabilization of testing medium.

cases.question: New gas piping is installed in a public corridor. The contractor proposes a 5-psig pressure test for 30 minutes. Is that sufficient?
cases.reviewNote: The 10-psig/30-minute corridor result is supported. The response broadens into whether the corridor installation is permitted and asks for plans proving an installation exception, although the asked comparison concerns test pressure. Retain a bounded installation qualification without turning this into a general installation-readiness checklist.

reviewedAnswer.answerText:
**No.** For gas piping installed in a public corridor in accordance with FGC § 404, the required test is **10 psig for at least 30 minutes**; therefore, the proposed 5-psig/30-minute test fails the required pressure even though its duration matches. The test must use air or an inert gas, with the pressure source isolated before readings, and the 30-minute period begins only after the test medium stabilizes (FGC § 406.4.1). Before service, piping must be tested gas-tight and inspected and pressure-tested before acceptance and initial operation (FGC §§ 404.20, 406.1).

The corridor installation itself must also be authorized under FGC § 404: gas piping is generally prohibited in public corridors, subject to the stated fire-resistance-rated assembly exception or the specified residential/mixed-use exception. If the pipe is coated and wrapped, the more stringent **100 psig for 60 minutes** requirement applies; meter piping may instead be subject to the serving utility’s certified testing requirements (FGC §§ 404.3, 406.4.1).

cases.question: Can an ordinary shutoff valve be used as the sole bulkhead between a gas-filled portion of a piping system and an adjacent portion being pressure tested?
cases.reviewNote: The single-valve prohibition, double-block-and-bleed/flange exception and section-test safeguards match the supplied provision. A second paragraph repeats general pre-service testing and inspection rules, and four supporting points prolong this narrow bulkhead answer.

A valve also cannot be subjected to test pressure unless the piping upstream of it has been deenergized; the portion not pressure-tested must be checked with a noncorrosive leak-detecting fluid or another approved leak-detecting method. cases.question: A short run of gas piping is strapped to a nearby domestic-water pipe because there is no convenient structural support above. Is that acceptable if the water pipe is strong enough?
cases.reviewNote: The prohibition on supporting gas piping by other piping directly answers the stated water-pipe arrangement and is correctly cited. Detailed support standards, spacing and a request for MSS SP-58/Section 415 expand the answer beyond that resolved prohibition.

reviewedAnswer.answerText:
No. Even if the domestic-water pipe is strong enough, the 2022 NYC Fuel Gas Code expressly provides that gas piping “shall not be supported by other piping.” The gas piping must instead be supported by an allowed metal support, hanger, bracket, band, hook, or building structural component suitable for the pipe size and of adequate strength and quality, installed at intervals that prevent or damp out excessive vibration. It must also be anchored to prevent undue strain on connected appliances, and the supports must comply with the stated installation conditions. (FGC § 407.2)

The supplied evidence also references MSS SP-58 and FGC § 415 for hanger/support requirements, but does not provide their contents; those details cannot be evaluated from this evidence alone.

It must also be anchored to prevent undue strain on connected appliances, and the supports must comply with the stated installation conditions. (FGC § 407.2)

cases.question: A contractor proposes a listed flexible gas connector between the branch piping and a gas-fired water heater. The connector is less than six feet long and is in the same room. Is it permitted?

cases.question: A central system serving two dwelling units is designed to use return air from Apartment A as part of the ventilation air supplied to Apartment B. Is that permitted?

cases.question: Can conditioned air transferred from an adjacent occupied office be used as makeup air for a mechanically exhausted toilet room?

The response imports the recirculation rule into transfer-air reasoning and asks for air available after accounting for required office outdoor air, although its cited transfer-air provision permits required outdoor air to be introduced into the source occupied space. Public/private fixture-count detail is also beyond the narrow permission question.

reviewedAnswer.answerText:
**Yes—conditionally.** Conditioned air transferred from an adjacent occupied office may serve as makeup air for a mechanically exhausted toilet room, because air transferred from occupiable spaces is expressly allowed for that purpose unless recirculation from the source space is prohibited by Table 403.3.1.1 (MC § 403.2.2). The office’s required outdoor air cannot itself be recirculated; only air in excess of the office’s required outdoor air may be recirculated, subject to the listed restrictions (MC § 403.2.1).

For a public toilet room, the table requires 50 cfm per water closet or urinal for continuous exhaust, or 70 cfm per fixture for intermittent exhaust; the higher rate applies for intermittent operation (MC Table 403.3.1.1, note e). The available evidence does not establish the toilet room’s fixture count, exhaust operating mode, or the office outdoor-air and supply/transfer-airflow quantities needed to confirm a particular design.

cases.question: The only way to stop a building’s supply and return fans in an emergency is to operate the electrical disconnect at each fan. Does that satisfy the Mechanical Code’s manual ventilation-control requirement?
cases.reviewNote: The required manual emergency control, approved location and explicit disconnect-switch exclusion are correct. The main answer additionally cites MC 606.4.2 for automatic shutdown, but that reference has no returned citation or supporting point. It appears in retrieved-evidence metadata, so this is a returned citation/coverage gap, not proof that the source was never retrieved or that the underlying rule is false. Remove the unasked claim or bind its source.

reviewedAnswer.answerText:
**No.** A fan’s electrical disconnect does not satisfy the required emergency manual ventilation control. MC § 405.2 requires each air-distribution system to have at least one manual control, at an approved location, to stop its supply, return, and exhaust fan(s) in an emergency—and expressly states: A disconnect switch shall not be considered a manual control. MC § 606.5 applies that same requirement to manual fan controls.

A separate manual emergency-stop control is therefore required; fan-mounted disconnects alone are insufficient. This answers only the manual-control requirement. If the system is a recirculating-air system subject to MC § 606.4.2, separate automatic fan-shutdown requirements may also apply.

MC § 606.5 applies that same requirement to manual fan controls.

cases.question: To reduce the number of exterior penetrations, a designer proposes combining a residential clothes-dryer exhaust duct with a bathroom exhaust duct before the air reaches the exterior. Is that permitted?
cases.reviewNote: The answer applies the independent dryer-exhaust rule directly, rejects combining the bathroom duct, and cites the outdoor dryer termination requirement. The environmental-air cross-reference is bounded and does not reopen the controlling independent-dryer result.

No MC § 514 permission is supplied here. The dryer duct must instead terminate outdoors as its own exhaust path (MC § 504.4).

cases.question: A bathroom exhaust fan in a top-floor apartment discharges into a ventilated attic instead of directly outdoors. Is that acceptable because the attic itself has roof vents?
cases.reviewNote: The outdoor-discharge rule and express attic prohibition are correct, and the limited whole-house/private-attic exception is accurately distinguished from a bathroom fan. The exterior-location qualification remains conditional and does not treat attic roof vents as a compliant termination.

reviewedAnswer.answerText:
**No.** A bathroom exhaust fan may not discharge into a ventilated attic merely because the attic has roof vents. The listed attic exception is only for a whole-house ventilation-type attic fan serving a dwelling unit with a private attic—not a bathroom exhaust fan.

The duct should therefore continue to an outdoor termination, located so the exhaust will not cause a nuisance or be readily drawn back into a ventilating system. The supplied evidence does not establish the actual proposed outlet location or its required separation distances, which must be evaluated for the selected exterior termination. (MC §§ 501.3, 501.3.1.)

cases.question: An alteration is being designed under the optional 1968 Building Code provisions for a prior-code building. Does that election also allow new plumbing, fuel-gas, and mechanical work to be designed under the old technical requirements?
cases.reviewNote: The current technical-code exception to the optional 1968 Building Code election is correctly stated. The opening explanation introduces the separate pre-December-1968 law option without stating its multiple-dwelling/date scope there; the supporting point later provides those conditions. Keep the unasked historical path out of the lead or preserve its conditions at the claim. The fixture-count alternative and malformed bold spacing also lengthen the narrow answer.

reviewedAnswer.answerText:
**No.** The optional 1968 Building Code path for an alteration of a prior-code building does not extend to new plumbing, fuel-gas, or mechanical work. Although qualifying prior-code alterations may proceed under applicable pre-December 6, 1968 building laws and regulations at the owner’s option, the current code makes application of § 28-101.4.3 a minimum condition of that option. (AC § 28-102.4.3.)

Specifically, AC § 28-101.4.3, Exception 1, removes fuel-gas, plumbing, electrical, and mechanical work from that election: installation of and work on appliances, equipment, and systems regulated by the NYC Fuel Gas, Plumbing, Electrical, and Mechanical Codes ** shall be governed by applicable provisions of those codes relating to new and existing installations.** Thus, design the new plumbing, fuel-gas, and mechanical scope under the applicable current technical-code provisions for new or existing installations, as applicable—not under the 1968 technical requirements. (AC § 28-101.4.3.) A narrow plumbing-related allowance remains in the current Plumbing Code: for a prior-code building, the *number of required plumbing fixtures* may be calculated using either the 1968 Building Code occupant-load figures or the NYC Plumbing Code and its occupant-load figures. That limited fixture-count option does not authorize use of the former plumbing technical requirements for the new installation. (PC § 102.4.2.1.)

cases.question: A contractor is replacing a piece of mechanical equipment with a similar new unit. Because the work is “replacement in kind,” can the contractor assume that no DOB permit is required?
cases.reviewNote: The answer correctly says replacement in kind alone does not establish an exemption and requests the actual replacement scope. It expands into emergency procedure and a one-year permit-denial consequence, then asks whether the equipment is connected to a building. Those additions distract from the particular exemption determination and add unnecessary missing facts.

reviewedAnswer.answerText:
**No.** Replacement in kind is not, by itself, a listed permit exemption. The controlling rule makes it unlawful to erect, install, alter, repair, remove, convert or replace any … mechanical … system without a written DOB permit, unless an exemption in AC § 28-105.4 applies. (AC § 28-105.1)

AC § 28-105.4 lists permit-exempt categories, including emergency work and minor alterations/ordinary repairs, but the supplied text does not identify replacement in kind as a stand-alone exemption. (AC § 28-105.4; AC § 28-105.4.2) Thus, on the stated facts, the contractor cannot assume no permit is required merely because the new unit is similar.

An emergency allows work to proceed without a permit only to the extent necessary to relieve the emergency; a permit application is still due within **2 business days** after work starts, with a written description of the emergency and mitigation measures. (AC § 28-105.4.1) If required work is performed without a permit in an occupied building, the code also provides for a potential one-year permit denial following the commissioner’s determination, subject to stated exceptions. (AC § 28-105.1.5)

The supplied evidence does not define the scope of minor alterations and ordinary repairs for a mechanical-unit replacement. That determination—and whether a specific exemption applies—needs to be resolved before proceeding without a DOB permit.

cases.question: A building is required to provide four drinking fountains. The designer proposes four bottle-filling stations and no drinking fountains. Is that permitted?
cases.reviewNote: The answer preserves the 50-percent limit, two-fountain/two-filler result, faucet-height and adjacency/visibility conditions, and prohibition on bottled-water dispenser substitution in its supporting point. reviewedAnswer.answerText:
**No.** Four bottle-filling stations with no drinking fountains are not permitted as the substitution for four required drinking fountains. At most 50 percent may be replaced: for four required fountains, that permits **two** qualifying dedicated bottle-filling fixtures and still requires **two drinking fountains**. Each substituted fixture must be adjacent to or readily visible from a drinking fountain conforming to PC § 410.1. (PC § 410.3)

Further, drinking fountains required by Table 403.1 must have both a bubbler faucet and a separate container-filling faucet designed for a container at least 10 inches high. (PC § 410.1) Thus, a compliant arrangement could be two such drinking fountains plus two qualifying dedicated bottle-filling fixtures, subject to the specified adjacency/visibility condition. The supplied evidence does not establish the proposed stations’ fixture design or locations.

Each replacement bottle-filling fixture must have a faucet designed to fill a container at least 10 inches (254 mm) high (PC § 410.3).
